html:
Vinsenya is the mirna of fertility. She appears in the novel as a detail of Laerta’s urban life, rather than as a character.

The clock on the academy tower (ch. 3, 5)

Figurines of mirnas move around a circular balcony on the tower of the Academy of Arts. A white enameled sun is painted above the balcony. Vinsenya’s figurine passes beneath it at about two in the afternoon, marking the time. At three, Darreggio replaces her (ch. 5); the narrator ironically calls him a lazy fellow. Alvaro’s lecture begins around then.

The church of Vinsenya (ch. 11)

The road from central Laerta to the Service district, where Fernan lives, runs along the Northern Garden, past the church of Vinsenya, and across an arched bridge. This is the novel’s name for a Laertan church dedicated to the mirna.

Vinsenya on the walls (ch. 13)

In the factory district, colorful grotesque pictures are daubed on blank brick walls: a bull embracing a bullfighter, a fat woman chasing a frail little man, drunken mirnas, and Vinsenya “fast asleep, naked to the waist.” The narrator observes that this would look amusing on the white walls of seaside villas, but in a working-class neighborhood it only deepens the gloom.
